papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Direct RAS targeting has progressed from pharmacologic proof of concept to routine treatment for selected KRAS G12C-mutant cancers. KRAS G12C inhibitors and KRAS G12C-EGFR combinations established allele- and lineage-specific treatment paradigms. More recently, the multiselective RAS(ON) inhibitor daraxonrasib became the first FDA-approved direct RAS-targeted therapy for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, while the KRAS G12D-directed degrader setidegrasib remains investigational. Target engagement alone, however, does not ensure durable disease control, and the same drug class can perform differently across tumor lineages. MAIN BODY: This Review develops an adaptive RAS signaling ecosystem model in which allele and isoform biology, membrane organization, feedback architecture, mutant-wild-type RAS crosstalk, co-mutation patterns, chromatin state, epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, metabolism, spatial heterogeneity, the tumor microenvironment and treatment delivery jointly determine pathway dependence and therapeutic escape. Comparisons among pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, lung adenocarcinoma and NRAS-mutant melanoma show how related oncogenic RAS nodes acquire different vulnerabilities in distinct tissue contexts. We integrate direct RAS inhibition with mechanism-guided vertical and horizontal strategies directed at feedback rebound, bypass signaling, cell-state persistence, stromal protection, metabolic adaptation and immune exclusion. We then translate this model into a biomarker-integrated development framework that links serial circulating tumor DNA, modality-matched pharmacodynamic assays, paired tissue sampling, spatial profiling and toxicity-aware scheduling to prespecified, falsifiable treatment hypotheses. CONCLUSION: RAS dependence is conditional rather than absolute. Durable control will require strategies that match the RAS allele and tumor lineage to the dominant adaptive circuitry, verify that target and pathway suppression persist over time, and maintain sufficient dose intensity to exert biologically effective pressure without disabling antitumor immunity or normal-tissue function.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Primary KIT exon 13 and 17 mutations are rare in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs), and data on their response to imatinib are limited. We evaluated the clinical characteristics and outcomes. METHODS: We analyzed 1524 patients with metastatic or recurrent GIST treated with first-line imatinib between 2005 and 2024 at Asan Medical Center, Seoul, Korea. Objective response rate (ORR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS) were compared between the primary KIT exon 13 or 17 and exon 11 group. ORR was assessed only in patients with measurable lesions, whereas PFS and OS were analyzed in all patients. Germline sequencing was performed when available. RESULTS: Twenty-seven patients (1.8%) harbored primary KIT exon 13 (n = 20) or 17 (n = 7) mutations. ORR to imatinib tended to be lower for exon 13 (6/13, 46.2%) and exon 17 (1/3, 33.3%) than exon 11 (558/799, 69.8%; p = 0.144). Median PFS was 17.8, 18.6, and 57.1 months for exon 13, 17, and 11, respectively (p < 0.001); 24-month PFS rates were 37.9%, 33.3%, and 74.2%, respectively. The 24-month OS rates were 92.3%, 71.4%, and 94.8%. Of 19 patients tested, two harbored germline exon 13 mutations, including one with a family history. CONCLUSIONS: Imatinib showed modest clinical activity in GISTs harboring primary KIT exon 13 or 17 mutations and remains a reasonable first-line option in the absence of established alternatives, although outcomes were less favorable than in exon 11. Family history and germline sequencing should be considered in young patients with exon 13 mutations.

papers.abstract_en: PURPOSE: This Special Report analyzes current radiotherapy data standards, determines which radiotherapy data elements should propagate between them, and identifies the barriers to that propagation to improve interoperability and data utilization in clinical care and research. METHODS: We compared five data standards-OMOP, CDISC SDTM, FHIR, NAACCR, and the Operational Ontology for Oncology (O3)-and one ontology framework, the OBO Foundry, for radiotherapy data representation, strengths, limitations, and implementation maturity, and examined harmonization initiatives including NRG's O3-based conversion frameworks, CodeX mCODE, and ESTRO and IAEA efforts. We then scored a 90-item benchmark drawn from radiotherapy operational and trial-reporting requirements, partitioned the radiotherapy items by whether and where they should propagate, and matched each barrier to a remediation route and owning body. RESULTS: Counting only unqualified matches, O3 covered 46 of 62 radiotherapy-specific items (74%) versus 15 (24%) for OMOP, 12 (19%) for NAACCR, 11 (18%) for FHIR, and none for OBO Foundry; on the 28 general clinical items the ordering reversed (OMOP 79%, FHIR 71%, NAACCR 46%, O3 25%, OBO Foundry 4%). Each standard is strongest on the items its target function was built to serve. Wholesale propagation is therefore unwarranted: 20 course-summary elements should converge across standards, 26 planning and adaptive elements warrant selective adoption, and 16 voxel- and machine-level artifacts should be referenced by DICOM unique identifier rather than replicated. CONCLUSIONS: Harmonization requires ontology-driven approaches using O3 as the semantic backbone with mappings to FHIR, OMOP and CDISC, applied to a defined tier of elements rather than the full element set. The principal barriers are process barriers-structural, terminological, burden-related and tooling-related-each with a named owner and an existing route. Standardized formats alone are insufficient; they require robust information systems, validation, and governance. Harmonization improves real-world data utility but cannot resolve biases inherent to nonrandomized data. Coordinated international collaboration remains critical for advancing precision radiation oncology.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Cardiac toxicity is a well-recognized, but poorly understood complication of radiotherapy (RT). In non-oncological settings, there is an established relationship between resting heart rate and cardiovascular health. OBJECTIVES: To study the incidence and pattern of resting heart rate (rHR) as an early sign of cardiotoxicity among patients with non-metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treated with RT. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed serial rHR measurements of consecutive patients with locally advanced NSCLC treated with definitive chemoradiation (CRT) over 6-7 weeks of daily radiation treatments followed by immunotherapy (durvalumab) between 2017-2022. Radiation dose to the heart and 17 cardiac substructures were extracted. Associations between heart rate elevation, tachycardia, cardiac substructure dose and outcomes were evaluated using generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) and regression analysis. RESULTS: We identified 110 patients, 56.4% with pre-existing heart disease. Median follow-up was 33.6 months. Median age was 70.4 years. Median rHR increased significantly during RT, rising from 81.5 bpm to 93 bpm at end of RT (p < 0.0001), remaining elevated in 30.6% of patients 12 months post-RT. Tachycardia incidence rose from 11.2% at baseline to 36.5% at 1-month post-RT (p < 0.0001). After adjusting for comorbidities, higher mean sinoatrial node (SAN) dose was associated with higher rHR elevation, delayed HR recovery and persistent tachycardia (all p < 0.05). Higher rHR during and after RT (β = 0.23, p = 0.005, and β = 13.49, p = 0.049, respectively), as well as the incidence of tachycardia episodes during RT were associated with increased odds of developing an arrhythmia (OR, 2.97, 95% CI, 1.17-7.52, p = 0.022). CONCLUSIONS: Elevated rHR and tachycardia are observed during and after RT for NSCLC and are associated with higher mean SAN dose. HR elevation was associated with increased risk of de novo arrhythmias, suggesting that heart rate may represent a non-invasive biomarker of subclinical cardiac injury. Prospective studies might be warranted to test the potential of routine HR monitoring and proactive dose reductions to the SAN to enable early detection and help mitigate the risk of post-treatment arrhythmia.

papers.abstract_en: INTRODUCTION: Tumor hypoxia has been recognized as a barrier to effective radiotherapy. Preclinical work identified the FDA approved smooth muscle relaxant papaverine (PPV) as having an "off target" activity as a mitochondrial inhibitor that reduces hypoxia and radiosensitizes model tumors. METHODS: We conducted an IRB-approved phase 1 clinical trial to evaluate safety and feasibility of adding PPV to stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) for tumors of the lung. Eligible patients with early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) or limited lung metastases who were candidates for SBRT (50 Gy in 4 or 5 fractions) were enrolled. Based on a Bayesian Optimal Interval (BOIN) design, patients were allocated to receive PPV 30-90 minutes prior to each SBRT fraction at 3 dose levels (DL): 0.5 mg/kg (DL-1), 1 mg/kg (DL1), or 2mg/kg (DL2). RESULTS: Nineteen patients enrolled and 18 completed study treatment and were evaluable, with a median follow up of 33.4 months. Among 18 evaluable patients, 7 had early-stage NSCLC, 2 had metastatic NSCLC, and 8 had lung metastases from other histologies. The maximum tolerated dose (MTD) was determined to be DL2, which had a dose limiting toxicity (DLT) rate posterior estimate of 0.17 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.53). The 2-year controls rates for local, regional and distant control were 100%, 94% and 82%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: We demonstrate the feasibility and safety of PPV as a hypoxic radiosensitizer for SBRT. The MTD for this patient population is at least 2 mg/kg of PPV. Encouraging clinical results indicate that further investigation of PPV's utility as a tumor-selective radiosensitizer is warranted.

papers.abstract_en: Inflammatory transcriptional responses mediated by NF-κB are diverse despite similar upstream activation signals. Because phosphorylation of the NF-κB subunit RelA/p65 promotes interaction with co-activators CREB-binding protein/E1A binding protein p300 (CBP/p300) and selectively affects gene expression, we asked whether this modification distinguishes regulatory architectures underlying distinct immune functions. In macrophages carrying a Rela Ser276Ala mutation, p65 phosphorylation at serine 276 (S276) was dispensable for NF-κB binding to primed enhancers but essential for recruitment to nucleosome-occluded regions lacking pre-bound transcription factors (TFs) and activating histone marks. Such latent enhancers required phosphorylated NF-κB to recruit CBP/p300, promote histone acetylation, and open chromatin. Genes linked to these enhancers, including inflammatory mediators, were selectively impaired in S276A macrophages. Although antiviral responses remained intact, Rela Ser276Ala mice resisted endotoxin shock but were susceptible to bacterial infection. Thus, NF-κB responses are functionally partitioned by enhancer architecture: phosphorylation-sensitive sites define a latent enhancer compartment with NF-κB-dominated regulatory architecture, whereas primed sites are embedded in broader networks of lineage-determining and inducible TFs, yielding distinct biological outputs.

papers.abstract_en: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is aggravated by overactivated pro-inflammatory M1 microglia. Although pterostilbene (PTE) possesses anti-oxidative and anti-neuroinflammatory activity, its therapeutic application in AD is limited by poor aqueous solubility and weak blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration. Here, we fabricated pterostilbene-loaded human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell exosomes (PTE-Exos) with enhanced BBB permeability via freeze-thaw loading. In vitro BBB and microglia-neuron co-culture models were used to evaluate targeting, immunomodulation, and neuroprotection, while Nrf2 loss-of-function assays and transgenic Caenorhabditis elegans AD strains enabled cross-species mechanistic verification. PTE-Exos efficiently cross the BBB in vitro and selectively accumulate in activated microglia, shifting CD86+ M1 cells toward the CD206+ anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines, restoring Aβ phagocytosis and alleviating Aβ-induced tau hyperphosphorylation and synaptic injury. Mechanistically, PTE-Exos simultaneously suppressed the NLRP3 inflammasome and NF-κB signaling and activated the Nrf2/HO-1 cascade to mitigate mitochondrial oxidative stress, and stabilized Nrf2 by attenuating its K48-linked polyubiquitination and prolonging its apparent half-life in a proteasome-dependent manner while preserving the KEAP1-Nrf2 complex. Nrf2 knockdown or pharmacological inhibition abolished these protective effects, and SKN-1 silencing eliminated PTE-Exos-mediated neuroprotection in C. elegans. Collectively, hUC-MSC exosomes resolve the pharmacokinetic limitation of PTE and remodel microglial phenotypes via the conserved Nrf2/SKN-1 axis, providing a biomaterial foundation for Nrf2-targeted nanotherapies against neuroinflammatory neurodegeneration.

papers.abstract_en: Neonatal sepsis often causes acute lung injury (ALI), but the underlying molecular mechanisms of ALI have not been elucidated. Pleckstrin homology-like domain family A member 3 (PHLDA3) is a stress-responsive protein involved in inflammatory signaling, yet its role in neonatal sepsis-associated ALI has not been explored. Here, we established a neonatal polymicrobial sepsis model via intraperitoneal injection of cecal slurry (CS) and investigated the role of PHLDA3 in ALI using CRISPR/Cas9-generated constitutive PHLDA3 knockout (PHLDA3 KO) mice. CS induced time-dependent upregulation of PHLDA3 in neonatal lung tissues. CS triggered significant increases in the levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α in lung tissues, impairing vascular integrity and causing severe alveolar damage. These harmful effects were alleviated by PHLDA3 KO. Transcriptomic analysis revealed enrichment of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) protein processing pathways. CS activated ER stress and unfolded protein response via PERK/eIF2α/ATF4 and ATF6 axes, which were attenuated by PHLDA3 deletion. Pharmacological induction of ER stress by thapsigargin (TG) reversed the protective effects of PHLDA3 KO, whereas ER stress inhibitor 4-phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) mitigated inflammation and lung injury. In macrophage models, PHLDA3 knockdown was associated with reduced LPS-induced ER-stress-related signaling, NF-κB activation, and inflammatory responses, whereas TG attenuated these effects. Collectively, these findings indicate that constitutive PHLDA3 deficiency is associated with attenuated neonatal sepsis-associated lung injury, reduced ER-stress-related signaling, and decreased NF-κB activation, and support further investigation of PHLDA3 in neonatal sepsis-associated ALI.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: SARS-CoV-2 spike binds angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), but the mechanisms linking spike exposure to intestinal injury remain incompletely understood. We investigated whether plasma-activated solutions (PAS) alleviate spike-associated intestinal injury by regulating antioxidant signaling. METHODS: Intestinal injury was induced by recombinant spike receptor-binding domain exposure in humanized ACE2 mice pretreated with dextran sulfate sodium. Caco-2 and HCT116 cells were used for in vitro experiments. PAS was administered orally to mice or applied as plasma-activated culture medium to cells. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, apoptosis, and tissue injury were assessed. Protein stability assays, co-immunoprecipitation, and pathway interventions were used to investigate the underlying mechanism. RESULTS: Spike exposure increased oxidative stress and epithelial apoptosis and enhanced the association between Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1) and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2), accompanied by increased NRF2 ubiquitination, reduced NRF2 stability, and lower heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) expression. PAS alleviated intestinal injury, reduced ROS accumulation and apoptosis, decreased KEAP1-NRF2 association, and increased NRF2 nuclear accumulation. NRF2 knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of HO-1 attenuated the protective effects of PAS. CONCLUSION: PAS alleviates spike-associated intestinal injury in the experimental models examined, with the findings supporting a contribution of KEAP1-NRF2/HO-1 signaling to its protective effects.

papers.abstract_en: Prey rely on chemical cues to detect predators, especially in coastal ecosystems where danger is concealed by turbid waters. Juvenile oysters (Crassostrea virginica) respond to blue crab (Callinectus sapidus) chemical cues by growing stronger shells, while mud crabs (Panopeus herbstii) reduce foraging to avoid detection. However, the chemical composition of marine fear cues is largely unknown, partly due to methodological challenges. In this study, metabolomics was used to pinpoint predator metabolites that correlated with induced juvenile oyster defenses when exposed to the urine of blue crabs fed either oysters or mud crabs and to determine the chemical composition of these fear cues. Genetic algorithms applied to urine mass spectra coupled with bioassay data confirmed that metabolites from blue crab urine are responsible for fear responses by oysters. Sixteen compounds (of over 700) were determined to be potentially important cues used by juvenile oysters to detect blue crabs, with 3-(1-methyl-1H-imidazol-4-yl) propanoic acid identified as the most important contributor to this effect. These results indicate that oysters rely on certain metabolites that are ubiquitous in a variety of chemical blends to evaluate predation risk, and the response of juvenile oysters is not dependent on a singular metabolite but on numerous metabolites working in conjunction.

papers.abstract_en: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) induces gastric precancerous lesions (GPL), but their underlying biomarkers remain poorly characterized. To establish a GPL model, BALB/c mice were inoculated with H. pylori via gavage. Immunofluorescence confirmed successful modeling by detecting H. pylori distribution and aberrant expression of precancerous lesion markers. Serum-based label-free proteomics and bioinformatic analyses were performed to screen key proteins. Data are available via ProteomeXchange (PXD076808). Western blot and immunofluorescence were used to verify key proteins and markers of DNA damage, fibrosis, and epithelial mesenchymal transition (EMT). The results revealed high H. pylori load in gastric mucosa with abnormal precancerous markers. Proteomic analysis identified 103 differentially expressed proteins and five core proteins as potential biomarkers, all overexpressed in gastric cancer. Col1a1, a fibrosis marker, was identified as a key upregulated protein and validated by Western blot and immunofluorescence. Col1a1 colocalized with the DNA damage marker γ-H2AX in gastric mucosa. H. pylori infection triggered DNA damage, fibrosis, and EMT in GPL. In conclusion, H. pylori induced DNA damage, fibrosis, and EMT in gastric mucosa, accelerating precancerous lesion progression, with Col1a1 playing a significant role.

papers.abstract_en: OBJECTIVE: The recent transition to the Composite Allocation Score (CAS) has increased travel distances for lung transplants, but an associated cost analysis has not been performed. We assessed travel costs and short-term outcomes of lung transplantation before and after transitioning to CAS. METHODS: The United Network for Organ Sharing database was queried for all lung transplants from 1/2020 to 12/2024. Redo and pediatric lung and multiorgan transplants were excluded. Patients were stratified between pre- and post-CAS, which began on 3/9/2023. Outcomes were distance of donor-to-recipient in nautical miles (nm), inflation-adjusted travel costs, and perioperative outcomes. RESULTS: A total of 7,835 (58.6%) pre-CAS and 5,538 (41.4%) post-CAS patients were included. Post-CAS patients were more likely female (41.7% vs. 38.5%, p<0.001), less likely White race (69.1% vs. 72.7%, p<0.001), and had shorter waitlist durations (28 vs. 33 days, p<0.001) compared to pre-CAS patients. Donor lungs were procured from greater distances in the CAS era (411 vs. 185 nm, p<0.001). Post-CAS, more procurements required flights (80.8% vs. 68.6%, p<0.001), and very long-distance procurements (>1000 nm) increased (10.7% vs. 2.0%, p<0.001). Travel costs increased, with median inflation-adjusted costs rising from $13,967 to $16,818; p<0.001. Ischemic times were longer post-CAS (7.1 vs. 5.7 hours, p<0.001). Importantly, one-year survival was similar pre- and post-CAS (88.9% vs. 90.1%, p=0.069). CONCLUSIONS: CAS has reduced waitlist duration with preserved one-year survival for lung transplant patients, but introduces greater logistical complexity and cost, which requires continued reevaluation to ensure economic viability and long-term sustainability of transplant programs.

papers.abstract_en: OBJECTIVE: Tricuspid valve surgery is neither complex nor time-consuming yet is associated with high surgical mortality. Our goal was to characterize heterogeneity of right heart variables and manifestations of right heart failure in patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation and evaluate survival after tricuspid valve surgery. METHODS: From 1/2007 to 1/2014, 522 adults with severe tricuspid regurgitation underwent cardiac surgery. Median follow-up was 3.7 years. Right heart morphology and function variables were measured de novo from stored echocardiographic images. To discover possible pheno-endotypes, unsupervised cluster analysis was performed by sidClustering.rfsrc using preoperative clinical, morphologic, ventricular function, and hemodynamic variables. Variable priority classification was used to characterize resulting pheno-endotypes. Post-surgery survival was assessed by cluster. RESULTS: Three pheno-endotype clusters were identified, each with distinct 10-year survival: Cluster 1 (n=220), predominantly patients with left-sided disease, 59%; Cluster 2 (n=78), predominantly patients with the most dilated right ventricles (diastolic area 42±10 cm2), 46%; and Cluster 3 (n=224), predominantly patients with worse right ventricular dysfunction (fractional area change 30%±12%), 21% (worst prognosis). Elevated model for end-stage liver disease with sodium was the most important predictor of time-related mortality and separated Clusters 1 and 2 from Cluster 3. CONCLUSIONS: Patients presenting for cardiac surgery with severe tricuspid regurgitation cluster into 3 pheno-endotypes, illustrating clinical presentation and patient heterogeneity and predicting distinctive prognosis. Right heart function and right heart failure severity need to be recognized to guide patient selection and management.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Intestinal strictures are one of the common late complications of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). Contrast studies are among the routinely used imaging modalities for screening post-NEC strictures. This systematic review with meta-analysis aimed to determine the diagnostic accuracy of contrast studies in diagnosing post-NEC strictures. METHODS: A literature search was conducted across four electronic databases - Scopus, PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Cochrane Library - for all relevant publications published through March 2026. Contingency table data were extracted from all the studies that met the inclusion criteria. The statistical software R version 4.5.3 was used to perform the statistical analysis. RESULTS: The literature search retrieved 582 references, among which 5 were included in the review. All the studies analyzed the diagnostic accuracy of contrast studies (contrast enema (CE) or distal loopogram) in the diagnosis of post-NEC strictures. CE has high diagnostic accuracy for post-NEC stricture, with sensitivities and specificities of 93.30% and 93.57%, respectively. The false-negative rate for CE was 6.70%. There were minimal adverse events during contrast studies, with only one case of iatrogenic perforation. CONCLUSION: Contrast studies demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy; however, they may miss a clinically relevant proportion of post-NEC strictures and do not consistently influence surgical decision-making. Therefore, contrast studies may not be relied upon as a standalone tool to safely exclude disease, and their routine use must be carefully reconsidered.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Early surgical referral for asymptomatic umbilical hernias in children is common despite recommendations to defer until 4-5 years of age. This study evaluated clinician perceptions and referral decision-making to identify opportunities for pediatric surgeon-led referral stewardship. METHODS: A sequential mixed-methods study was conducted among pediatric primary care clinicians in a statewide practice network. A web-based survey assessed referral timing, perceived risk of emergency operation, perceived likelihood of spontaneous closure, and factors influencing early referral. Semi-structured interviews were subsequently conducted using purposive sampling to explore drivers of referral variation. RESULTS: The survey response rate was 41% (244/592), representing 85% (71/83) of network practice groups. Overall, 18.0% reported routinely referring children with asymptomatic umbilical hernias at age 3 years or younger. Early-referring clinicians more frequently overestimated emergency operation risk (50.0% vs 30.7% estimating risk >1%; P=0.021) and underestimated spontaneous closure rate (90.9% vs 74.5% estimating rate <90%; P=0.022). Parental anxiety about incarceration influenced referral for 85.8% of respondents and was more frequently influential among early-referring clinicians (95.5% vs 80.4%; P=0.019). Qualitative interviews identified three central themes: parental anxiety as a primary driver of early referral, clinician role identity as a gatekeeper or facilitator of referrals, and the need for a strong collaborative relationship with surgeons in shaping referral behaviors. CONCLUSIONS: Early referral for asymptomatic umbilical hernia reflects modifiable knowledge, communication, and relationship-based factors. Pediatric surgeons can use these findings to develop referral guidance, caregiver education, and feedback interventions that support evidence-based observation and reduce potentially avoidable early consultation.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra (SN). Currently, there is a lack of effective therapies to slow disease progression. Temporal interference (TI) stimulation, as a novel non‑invasive neuromodulation technique, can generate a focused electric field in deep brain regions; however, whether it can effectively act on the SN and influence PD-related pathological processes remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To investigate the neuroprotective effects of TI stimulation on dopaminergic neurons in the SN of MPTP mice and explore the potential mechanisms involved. METHODS: After establishing a subacute MPTP model, TI stimulation with a 10 Hz beat frequency was applied to the SN of mice for five consecutive days. Therapeutic outcomes and molecular mechanisms were evaluated using behavioral tests, immunohistochemistry, Western blot, transcriptome sequencing, untargeted lipidomics, and primary neuronal culture experiments. RESULTS: TI stimulation significantly improved motor function in MPTP mice, increased the number of TH‑positive neurons in the SN, and attenuated glial activation and neuroinflammation. Integrated transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses revealed that TI intervention downregulated PLA2G3. Experimentally, TI reduced the expression of ACSL4, upregulated GPX4, decreased MDA levels, elevated reduced GSH levels, and suppressed lipid peroxidation. In vitro experiments further confirmed that TI reduced MPP⁺‑induced primary neuronal death and lipid peroxidation accumulation. CONCLUSION: TI stimulation protects nigral dopaminergic neurons by inhibiting lipid peroxidation, ameliorates motor deficits and pathological features in PD mice, and provides a novel strategy for non‑invasive neuromodulation therapy in PD. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Haematitum is a mineral-based traditional Chinese medicine widely used in clinical applications. Both the Chinese Materia Medica and modern research indicate that it exhibits lung toxicity and should not be administered over prolonged periods. The precise mechanism underlying this toxicity, however, remains incompletely understood. PURPOSE: This study aims to systematically elucidate the toxic mechanism of lung injury induced by Haematitum administration, emphasizing the central role of the gut-lung axis in this process. METHODS: The mouse model of lung injury induced by Haematitum was established. A combination of 16S rRNA sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, and single-cell RNA sequencing was utilized to comprehensively analyze alterations in the intestinal microbiota, lung tissue metabolism, and lung cell atlas. The pharmacological validation was conducted by administering PPARγ agonists and TNF-α inhibitors. Furthermore, the detoxification effect of its classical combination with Inula japonica Thunb. was also evaluated. RESULTS: High-dose Haematitum disrupted the intestinal barrier and induced dysbiosis. Metabolites from the gut microbiota entered the bloodstream and exerted a pathogenic effect. Correlation analysis showed that gut microbiota dysbiosis is strongly associated with the pulmonary glycerophospholipid metabolic pathway. Results from single-cell sequencing and macrophage/TNF-α colocalization experiments indicated that the macrophages' PPAR signaling pathway was inhibited, inactivating their anti-inflammatory function and triggering the release of inflammatory factors such as TNF-α. Acting as a key messenger, TNF-α activated the TNF signaling pathway in neutrophils, driving them to acquire a highly destructive phenotype. The synergy between macrophages and neutrophils ultimately provoked inflammation and cell apoptosis in lung tissue. Pharmacological intervention of the PPARγ/TNF-α axis can effectively reverse cellular abnormalities and significantly alleviate lung injury. The combination with Inula japonica Thunb. also reduced lung toxicity, and components within this herb are predicted to act as natural PPARγ agonists. CONCLUSIONS: This study has revealed a potential toxic mechanism. The intestinal barrier in mice was compromised, with an increase in the relative abundance of Klebsiella, entry of microbial metabolites into the bloodstream, and disruption of glycerophospholipid metabolism in the lungs, which in turn resulted in dysfunction of pulmonary immune cells. It clarifies that the core mechanism of Haematitum-induced lung injury lies in inhibiting the PPAR signaling pathway in macrophages and activating the TNF signaling pathway in neutrophils. Administering Haematitum at a common dose or in combination with Inula japonica Thunb. mitigates these safety risks. These findings advance understanding of the toxicology of mineral-based medicines and provide a reference for the safe clinical application of these traditional Chinese medicines.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: FHL2 is an oncogenic scaffold protein that is overexpressed in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), making it a promising therapeutic target. SHK, a natural naphthoquinone, exhibits antitumor activity, but its molecular mechanism in LUAD, particularly its relationship with FHL2, remains unclear. AIM OF THIS STUDY: The present study aimed to define the effects of SHK on NSCLC and identify the potential underlying molecular mechanisms. METHODS: The anti-tumor effects of SHK were evaluated in LUAD cell lines (A549andH1299) and a patient-derived xenograft (PDX) model using CCK-8, colony formation, Transwell, and flow cytometry assays. Integrated proteomics, bioinformatics, molecular docking, and cellular thermal shift assays (CETSAs) were employed to identify the direct target of SHK. The underlying mechanism was investigated through co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), Western blotting, qRT-PCR, cycloheximide (CHX) chase assays, and immunofluorescence/immunohistochemiscal (IF/IHC) staining. RESULTS: In both in vitro and PDX models, SHK potently inhibited LUAD growthand metastasisand induced cell death. At the molecular level, FHL2 was identified as a direct target of SHK. The direct binding of SHK to FHL2 promoted its proteasomal degradation, thereby disrupting the FHL2-FOXO1 complex. The dissociation of this complex increased FOXO1 acetylation and promoted its nuclear translocation, leading to the subsequent activation of the caspase cascade and apoptosis. CONCLUSION: Our findings indicate a novel signaling pathway through which SHK inhibits LUAD: by directly targeting FHL2 for degradation, SHK disrupts the FHL2-FOXO1 complex, which activates FOXO1-mediated transcription and triggers apoptosis. This study not only provides mechanistic insight into the antitumor function of SHK but also identifies the FHL2-FOXO1 axis as a potential therapeutic target for LUAD.

papers.abstract_en: OBJECTIVE: Lung cancer screening (LCS) with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces lung cancer-specific and all-cause mortality, yet uptake remains low. This study evaluates LungCheck, a theory-informed multicomponent behavior change and implementation strategy designed to increase LDCT ordering in two diverse primary care settings. METHODS: This pilot study compared 16-month pilot and pre-pilot periods at a federally qualified health center (FQHC) and an academic faculty practice in New York City. LungCheck comprised educational meetings, materials and clinician reminders, an implementation blueprint, patient navigation, and EHR modifications. LDCT ordering rates (primary outcome) were compared using generalized estimating equations (GEE). Post-implementation surveys assessed acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility. RESULTS: A total of 5,918 patient-period observations were included (1,569 academic; 4,349 FQHC). Among patients with documented LCS eligibility, the odds of LDCT ordering were significantly higher during the pilot at both the academic practice (OR, 2.67; 95% CI, 1.47-4.85; p=0.001) and FQHC (OR, 4.53; 95% CI, 2.29-8.94; p<0.001). A combined-site multivariable model adjusting for site, age, sex, and race confirmed higher odds of LDCT ordering during the pilot (OR, 1.95; 95% CI, 1.44-2.63; p<0.001). Among patients with an LDCT order, completion was 71.4% (10/14) pre-pilot versus 35.7% (15/42) during the pilot at the academic practice and 42.9% (18/42; 95% CI, 28%-59%) versus 39.3% (24/61; 95% CI, 27%-53%) at the FQHC. The strategy was rated as highly acceptable (AIM, 4.47/5), appropriate (IAM, 4.44/5), and feasible (FIM, 4.41/5). DISCUSSION: LungCheck was associated with significantly increased LDCT ordering at both sites, high acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness ratings and high provider knowledge, confidence, and perceived skills related to LCS. Although a corresponding improvement in LDCT completion was not observed, the small number of LDCT orders limited the precision of completion estimates. Persistent environmental and patient-level barriers underscore the need to adapt LungCheck into a multilevel intervention addressing patient-, provider, and system-level barriers across the LCS continuum, to be evaluated in a future cluster randomized trial.

papers.abstract_en: HNF4α-positive, TTF-1-negative lung adenocarcinomas represent a major subset of non-terminal respiratory unit (non-TRU) tumors with gastrointestinal-type differentiation and frequent KRAS mutations; however, their structural and microenvironmental diversities remain unclear. We herein examined 114 HNF4α-positive lung adenocarcinomas, including tumors with and without interstitial pneumonia (IP). IP-associated cases were analyzed separately. Tumors were classified into three low-power architectural patterns: Alveolar-preserving (A-type), Radial-traction (R-type), and Mass-forming destructive (M-type). In IP-absent cases, in which it was possible to reliably evaluate tumor contours and the mass effect, these architectural patterns closely corresponded to the three computed tomographic growth patterns defined by tumor-lung interactions-Replacement, Spiculated, and Expansive growth-indicating the potential of computed tomographic morphology to serve as a surrogate for the underlying architecture. A-type tumors showed strong gastric differentiation with high MUC6 expression and low frequencies of pleural, lymphatic, and vascular invasion, whereas R-type and M-type tumors exhibited progressively lower MUC6 expression, more prominent intestinal differentiation, and higher rates of lymph node metastasis, particularly in M-type, representing more aggressive phenotypes. KRAS mutations were detected across all three patterns but were less frequent in M-type; KRAS G12C was enriched in A-type tumors. M-type tumors showed the poorest disease-free and overall survival irrespective of spread through air spaces (STAS) status. Despite their indolent-appearing architecture, among STAS-positive tumors, A-type was associated with worse disease-free and overall survival than R-type, identifying STAS-positive A-type as a high-risk subset within the HNF4α-positive non-TRU spectrum. RNA sequencing further identified three distinct gene expression clusters corresponding to epithelial-mesenchymal transition-related, angiogenic/tumor-associated macrophage-rich, and mucinous epithelial programs. STAS-positive A-type tumors predominantly belonged to the angiogenic/tumor-associated macrophage-rich group, implicating this microenvironment in their aggressive behavior. Since STAS-positive A-type tumors may present as radiologically indolent replacement-growth lesions, careful evaluation of resected specimens and close postoperative surveillance are warranted.

papers.abstract_en: The rise of antibiotic resistance, particularly among pathogens such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, necessitates innovative antibacterial strategies. Here we introduce FibriLysins, a class of engineered enzymes combining staphylokinase and endolysin, which dismantle fibrin-encapsulated multicellular staphylococcal communities, including biofilms and staphylococcal abscess communities (SACs). We characterized diverse staphylokinases, developing a library of 27 FibriLysins, with a 78% positive hit rate. The lead variant, FL-028, has significant antibacterial activity against prevalent clinical S. aureus isolates. In vitro, FL-028 reduced bacterial counts in SACs by 3.4 log and in biofilms by 2.3 log. In vivo, FL-028 exhibits superior efficacy in a mouse model of bone fracture-related infection, outperforming vancomycin by 1 log and eliminating SAC presence in tissues. FL-028 shows no adverse effects on bone healing, as confirmed by histological examination, mechanical testing and micro-computed tomography analyses. These preclinical findings highlight the potential of FibriLysins as a robust and safe therapeutic approach against difficult-to-treat staphylococcal infections.

papers.abstract_en: INTRODUCTION: Cervical cancer disproportionately affects women in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where limited healthcare infrastructure often shifts caregiving responsibilities to informal companions such as family members, spouses, and friends. The goal of this scoping review is to map and summarize the social and economic impacts of cervical cancer on the caregivers for women diagnosed with cervical cancer in LMICs. METHODS: Three databases were searched up to March 30, 2026. Studies were included if they were conducted in a LMIC, included caregivers or companions of cervical cancer patients, and reported on social or financial outcomes. Outcomes were categorized into social impacts (psychosocial burden, education, social support, and sexual relationships) and economic impacts (employment and financial security). RESULTS: Fifteen unique studies from 11 countries were included (11 cross-sectional and 4 qualitative), and caregiver sample sizes ranged from 7 to 360. Caregivers were predominantly middle-aged, with low to moderate educational attainment and income. Up to 72.1% of caregivers experienced high levels of psychosocial burden. Educational disruptions were reported, with up to 28% of households reporting difficulties paying for education and school absences among family members. Social support experiences varied, with most caregivers reporting stable family relationships but some reporting neglect of other family members. Employment was significantly disrupted, with up to 61% of companions reducing working hours and 28% of households having a member stop working entirely. Financial hardship was pervasive: up to 39% of households experienced partial or total income loss, and coping strategies included selling assets, reducing food consumption, and accumulating debt. CONCLUSION: Cervical cancer inflicts substantial social and financial consequences on caregivers in LMICs, spanning psychosocial distress, educational disruption, employment loss, and financial hardship. These impacts are shaped by gender dynamics and intergenerational caregiving roles. As the global community pursues cervical cancer elimination, policies integrating caregiver support are essential.

papers.abstract_en: PURPOSE: To quantify inter-physician contouring variability and evaluate its dosimetric impact in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients treated with daily online adaptive MR-guided stereotactic body radiotherapy (MRgSBRT), to assess safety and clinical robustness of online contouring. METHODS: Fifty treatment sessions from ten PDAC patients treated with 50 Gy in five fractions on a 1.5 T MR-Linac were retrospectively analyzed. During each treatment session ("online"), targets and organs-at-risk (OARs) within 3 cm of the tumor were delineated by seven physicians working on the MR-Linac. All structures were re-contoured offline by a single pancreatic-expert radiation oncologist ("reference"). Geometric agreement was assessed using Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), Mean Distance to Agreement (MDA), and 95 % Hausdorff Distance (HD95). Dosimetric analyses were performed on delivered treatment plans using both online and reference contours, with evaluation based on fraction-wise worst-case dose metrics. RESULTS: High geometric concordance was observed for stomach and duodenum, whereas smaller or anatomically complex structures (GTV, major vessels, bile duct) showed greater variability. Online GTVs were larger than reference contours. Despite these differences, target coverage (V50Gy and V35Gy) was maintained with online contours. While occasional per-fraction gastrointestinal (GI) dose constraint exceedances were identified using reference contours, fraction-wise worst-case analysis showed GI doses remained within clinical tolerance for nearly all patients. CONCLUSION: Daily online adaptive MRgSBRT for PDAC provides robust target coverage and clinically acceptable OAR sparing, despite contouring variability. Multi-physician online contouring appears safe in clinical practice, although further improvements may be achieved through standardized contouring guidelines and harmonization strategies.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Patient-reported outcomes (PRO) capture patients' self-reported and treatment-related experiences, including functional impairment, symptoms, and health-related quality of life (HRQOL). Although PRO have shown benefits in many studies and are recommended by guidelines, systematic PRO assessment is still rarely integrated into routine cancer care. This paper describes results of the long-term implementation of electronic PRO assessment (ePRO) in the routine workflow of a radiation oncology inpatient clinic by analyzing patients' HRQOL at admission. METHODS: Admission ePRO included the EORTC QLQ-C30. PRO data were analyzed descriptively and stratified by sex, age, and primary tumor diagnosis. RESULTS: The sample included 1,423 patients. More than half reported clinically important burden in physical and emotional functioning and fatigue. Male patients tended to report better functioning and lower symptom burden. Older patients reported greater burden in physical functioning, appetite loss, and constipation but less burden in social functioning and financial problems. Global health status showed little to no differences by sex, age, or tumor diagnosis. CONCLUSIONS: The analyses showed substantial self-reported functional impairment and symptom burden at admission in inpatient radiation oncology and highlight the value of ePRO for identifying needs early, when patients' clinical status is not yet well known to the care team. At the organizational level, these results can help set priorities for supportive care during hospitalization and support more efficient resource allocation. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable, the analysis used only PRO data collected as part of routine care in the inpatient radiation oncology clinic (see also the declaration of no objection).

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Valvular heart disease (VHD) lacks disease-modifying pharmacological therapies. Drug repurposing guided by human genetics may help identify therapeutic opportunities. We aimed to integrate human genetic associations, drug-target information, and clinical evidence to identify repurposing opportunities and prioritise potentially druggable targets across the VHD spectrum. METHODS: We retrieved VHD-associated genetic variants from the NHGRI-EBI Genome-Wide Association Studies Catalogue and Ensembl, interrogated annotated genes in the Open Targets Platform, and evaluated linked drugs through structured searches of MEDLINE and ClinicalTrials.gov. The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251071741). FINDINGS: We identified 1464 genetic associations corresponding to 844 unique variants and 582 candidate genes. Of these genes, 431 had tractability information and 51 had linked compounds, comprising 388 distinct pharmacological agents, 273 in phase 3 or 4 of clinical development. Drug-linked targets were concentrated in aortic stenosis. Clinical evidence supported therapeutic potential for 14 drugs, with preclinical or mechanistic cardiovascular support for eight additional drugs and adverse cardiovascular signals for four. An exploratory evidence-weighted framework prioritised targets according to genetic-functional evidence, tissue and mechanistic context, and translational tractability. INTERPRETATION: This genetics-informed evidence synthesis identifies drug-repurposing opportunities and a substantial gap between genetically supported targets and available therapies. The findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework for mechanistic validation and future valve-focused studies. FUNDING: Limburg Clinical Research Centre of UHasselt, Jessa and ZOL; British Heart Foundation; National Institute for Health and Care Research; UK Research and Innovation; European Research Council; Horizon Europe.

papers.abstract_en: Radon exposure is the leading cause of lung cancer among nonsmokers, posing a significant public health risk. Despite its known dangers, population-wide exposure assessments of indoor radon have been limited by the reliance on area-based summaries, such as average and median concentrations, which ignore the distributional characteristics of small areas. This study developed a national-scale modeling framework to estimate ZIP Code Tabulation Area (ZCTA)-level distributions of indoor radon concentrations across the contiguous United States from 2000 to 2021. We utilized over six million short-term radon measurements, which were aggregated at the ZCTA level to predict percentiles. By further modeling within-ZCTA radon exposure distributions, we improved the quantification of exposure heterogeneity and were able to estimate the proportion and number of residents exceeding policy-relevant exposure thresholds more accurately. The results reveal that approximately half of U.S. ZCTAs have at least one in five households exposed to radon concentrations exceeding the Environmental Protection Agency's action level (148 Bq/m3), with high-exposure areas predominantly located in the Midwest. These findings provide crucial data to help residents recognize their potential radon risk, urge policymakers to design cost-effective interventions, and offer health researchers an essential database for incorporating within-ZCTA radon exposure distributions into health risk assessments.

papers.abstract_en: PURPOSE: Pemetrexed, a standard antifolate chemotherapy for non-squamous non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), is often limited by acquired resistance. We investigated whether SRC kinase mediates pemetrexed resistance and whether SRC inhibition can suppress survival signaling in pemetrexed-resistant NSCLC cells. METHODS: Pemetrexed-resistant cell lines (PC9 R, NCI-H460 R, and NCI-H3122 R) were generated through chronic pemetrexed exposure. Protein phosphorylation profiling and Western blotting identified key signaling alterations. SRC was abrogated using transient and doxycycline-inducible CRISPR/Cas9 systems, and reciprocal siRNA knockdown of SRC and thymidylate synthase (TS) was performed. Three SRC inhibitors-dasatinib, bosutinib, and saracatinib-were assessed using cell viability, colony formation, apoptosis, and cell cycle assays. RESULTS: All pemetrexed-resistant cell lines demonstrated elevated phosphorylated SRC (p-SRC Y416) and enhanced downstream signaling. SRC knockout reduced p-SRC Y416, p-STAT3, and p-FAK, while increasing markers of DNA damage (γ-H2AX) and apoptosis (cleaved caspase-3), impairing cell viability and clonogenicity. SRC knockdown reduced TS expression in two resistant models, whereas TS knockdown did not suppress p-SRC Y416. Among SRC inhibitors, dasatinib showed the most potent, dose-dependent suppression of SRC signaling. Dasatinib also induced G0/G1 arrest, DNA damage, and apoptosis, thereby reducing colony formation. CONCLUSION: SRC activation is a critical mechanism of acquired pemetrexed resistance in NSCLC and may contribute to resistance through TS-associated survival signaling. SRC inhibition, particularly with dasatinib, disrupts pro-survival pathways and promotes DNA damage-mediated cell death in pemetrexed-resistant cells. These findings support further investigation of SRC inhibitors, alone or with pemetrexed, as a biomarker-guided therapeutic strategy for SRC-activated pemetrexed-resistant NSCLC.

papers.abstract_en: Emerging evidence indicates that long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are critical regulators of tumor radiosensitivity and hold promise as novel targets for radiosensitization. However, the underlying mechanisms by which most lncRNAs modulate radiosensitivity remain elusive. This study aimed to elucidate the functional significance and mechanistic basis of lncRNA MIR4435-2HG in regulating non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) radiosensitivity. Our findings demonstrated that ionizing radiation induced upregulation of lncRNA MIR4435-2HG. High expression of MIR4435-2HG was significantly associated with poor prognosis in patients with lung adenocarcinoma. Inhibition of MIR4435-2HG increased the radiosensitivity of NSCLC cells. Mechanistically, MIR4435-2HG acted as a competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) to sponge miR-1-3p, thereby derepressing DNA-PKcs at both mRNA and protein levels. Knockdown of MIR4435-2HG impaired non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) repair, as evidenced by increased 53BP1 and γH2AX foci, reduced interaction of DNA-PKcs with Ku70 and XRCC4, and decreased NHEJ repair efficiency. Conversely, overexpression of MIR4435-2HG induced a radioresistant phenotype. Dual-luciferase reporter assays confirmed the interaction between miR-1-3p and both MIR4435-2HG and DNA-PKcs. Rescue experiments confirmed that miR-1-3p overexpression reversed MIR4435-2HG-mediated DNA-PKcs upregulation, proliferation enhancement, and radioresistance. Notably, MIR4435-2HG selectively promoted error-prone NHEJ without affecting homologous recombination. In summary, our study delineates a novel and functionally specific ceRNA axis wherein MIR4435-2HG sequesters miR-1-3p to upregulate DNA-PKcs and selectively activate NHEJ-mediated DSB repair. These findings not only introduce a critical regulatory node into the DNA repair network but also position the MIR4435-2HG/miR-1-3p/DNA-PKcs axis as a promising predictive biomarker and therapeutic target for overcoming radioresistance in NSCLC.

papers.abstract_en: Ferroptosis represents a promising therapeutic strategy for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), but its efficacy is often limited by intrinsic metabolic defenses. Herein, arachidonic acid (AA) acts as a potent sensitizer for class I histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor-induced ferroptosis. Guided by the binding mode of the lead compound with HDAC1, we developed a library of HDAC inhibitors, from which L17h was identified as a novel and highly selective HDAC1 inhibitor. Mechanistically, L17h-mediated HDAC1 inhibition transcriptionally upregulated acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) expression, which primed cells to metabolize supplemental AA and drove massive lipid peroxidation (LPO), leading to profound sensitization to ferroptosis. Crucially, this epigenetically primed ferroptosis elicited robust immunogenic cell death (ICD), promoting dendritic cell (DC) maturation and intratumoral T cell infiltration for systemic antitumor immunity. This work unveils crosstalk between epigenetics and fatty acid metabolism, proposing a combinatorial targeted strategy for ferroptosis-based immunotherapy in ESCC.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Sarcopenia is associated with poor postoperative outcomes in patients with malignant tumors; however, its impact on perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (pCCA) patients remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the predictive value of sarcopenia for postoperative outcomes in patients undergoing resection for pCCA. METHODS: A total of 271 patients with perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (pCCA) who underwent surgical intervention between 2016 and 2021 were retrospectively recruited from two institutions. The patients were divided into training and validation cohorts at a 7:3 ratio. Sarcopenia was defined via cutoff values for the skeletal muscle index (SMI) of 52.2 cm²/m² for males and 39.2 cm²/m² for females, which were determined through optimal stratification. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards regression were employed to identify significant risk factors associated with postoperative outcomes. Additionally, a novel nomogram based on sarcopenia was developed and subsequently validated via receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration curves, and clinical decision curve analysis (DCA). RESULTS: Of the 271 patients studied, 144 (53.1%) were diagnosed with sarcopenia. Patients with sarcopenia presented significantly higher rates of total complications, major complications, and 90-day readmissions, as well as poorer overall survival (OS), than did those without sarcopenia. multivariable Cox regression analysis revealed several independent risk factors for OS, including body mass index (BMI) (p = 0.026), high performance status (PS) score (p < 0.001), R1 surgical margin (p < 0.001), T stage IV (p < 0.001), COUNT score ≥ 5 (p = 0.005), and the presence of sarcopenia (p < 0.001). A novel nomogram incorporating these six factors was developed to predict OS at 12, 24, and 36 months. The model exhibited robust predictive performance, with a mean area under the curve (AUC) greater than 0.8. The calibration curve closely matched the ideal curve, and decision curve analysis (DCA) further validated the strong predictive ability and substantial positive net benefit of the nomogram. CONCLUSION: Sarcopenia is a significant adverse factor for both postoperative complications and long-term survival in patients with pCCA following surgical resection.

papers.abstract_en: OBJECTIVE: Cancer research registries are critical for ensuring representative participation in clinical trials. However, registries based primarily in hospitals may under-enroll women and other populations who experience structural, logistical, cultural, and informational barriers to care and research participation. Community-based organizations (CBOs) may help address this gap by developing registries that engage diverse populations of women at increased risk for and surviving with breast cancer more directly. The purpose of this study was to examine demographic, clinical, and organizational (i.e., engagement related) factors associated with women's interest in joining a CBO-led breast cancer research registry to support clinical trial access and representation. METHODS: Secondary analyses were conducted on repeated cross-sectional surveys (2022-2024) administered to women who contacted a national breast cancer-focused CBO for information and support (n=2,389). Measured variables included demographics, cancer risk, quality of life, patient navigation, empowerment, CBO care quality, social media use, and interest in registry participation; bivariate tests, ANOVAs, and MANCOVAs were used to assess associations. RESULTS: Nearly half of women expressed interest in joining the registry (46.2%), while 17.0% were unsure and 36.8% declined. Interest was greater among younger women, those at higher cancer risk, and those who had a more beneficial experience with the CBO (e.g., better patient navigation, greater empowerment, higher care quality). Greater digital engagement with the CBO (e.g., webinar attendance, frequent social media use, and viewing the CBO's social media content) was also strongly associated with registry interest (p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: CBOs have a unique role in fostering breast cancer research participation. Specific digital approaches (i.e., educational webinars, regularly updated social media content, online pathways that allow interested or uncertain individuals to request follow-up) may extend trusted CBO relationships into registry recruitment and help broaden representation in clinical trials.

papers.abstract_en: Exon 19 mutations in the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) kinase domain, including the common ΔE746-A750 deletion and the less frequent L747P substitution, are clinically important drivers of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Although these mutations occur within the β3-αC region, how they alter EGFR conformational dynamics and influence the response to the covalent inhibitor afatinib remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated mutation-dependent changes in EGFR conformational ensembles, dual-mode of afatinib binding, and Cys797-mediated covalent reaction energetics in wild-type, ΔE746-A750, and L747P kinase domains. We find that both mutations preferentially stabilize active-like kinase conformations but do so through distinct structural mechanisms. The ΔE746-A750 deletion produces greater P-loop and ATP-pocket conformational heterogeneity, whereas L747P restricts αC-helix and activation-loop dynamics and more strongly stabilizes the active-like ensemble. Afatinib binding disrupts the K745-E762 interaction and alters the αC-helix conformation while the pre-formed covalent state samples αC-out configurations that increase accessibility of an αC-adjacent pocket that is less accessible in the apo state. Alchemical calculations further reveal mutation- and protonation-state-dependent differences in the conditional noncovalent binding free energy of afatinib. QM/MM calculations of Cys797-afatinib bond formation reveal mutation-dependent differences in the calculated reaction barrier, with L747P showing a lower barrier than ΔE746-A750 within the employed QM/MM model. Together, these results show that EGFR exon 19 mutations reshape the conformational landscape and local structural environment of the kinase, thereby influencing afatinib binding and the energetic environment of covalent bond formation. These findings provide a structural framework for understanding how distinct EGFR mutations can produce different responses to covalent kinase inhibition.

papers.abstract_en: In recent years, spectroscopic technology has become a key tool in clinical diagnosis. However, the traditional single-modal spectral analysis method often struggles to capture the full biochemical complexity of heterogeneous biological samples, resulting in limited chemical interpretability and diagnostic sensitivity. To address these challenges, a novel multimodal spectroscopic analysis framework called DeepSpectrum is proposed. It combines the Spectral Mamba and bidirectional gated recurrent unit architectures to enable high-precision lung cancer diagnosis. Specifically, the spectral signals are converted into multichannel image modalities using the continuous wavelet transform (CWT) and Gramian angular difference fields (GADF), thereby constructing rich multimodal data sets. Subsequently, the DeepSpectrum framework is trained, validated, and tested on multimodal spectral data sets, including Raman, Fourier transform infrared, UV-vis absorbance, and fluorescence spectra. It achieved accuracy rates of 98.1%, 98.5%, 92.0%, and 89.2% in lung cancer diagnosis, demonstrating broad applicability across spectral types and complex biological samples. Compared with 11 existing single-modal and multimodal methods, DeepSpectrum showed clear advantages across all evaluation metrics. To further explain the model's decision-making basis, weighted class activation mapping is used to analyze the spectral signals of normal and cancer samples. The model focuses on key regions such as 1127-1375 cm-1 (heme/hemoglobin vibrations) and 1447 cm-1 (lipid metabolism) in Raman spectra, as well as 1000-1140 cm-1 (nucleic acids) in FTIR spectra. These peak values correspond to the evolution process of lung cancer. This not only validates the biochemical interpretability of the DeepSpectrum model but also provides a reliable diagnostic tool for the precise clinical identification of lung cancer.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: For clinical stage I non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), treatment selection between surgery and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) can be preference sensitive. Accordingly, we developed a web-based patient decision aid (PDA) and prospectively evaluated its patient-reported utility in routine respiratory clinical practice. METHODS: This prospective pilot study enrolled 26 patients with clinical stage I NSCLC or suspected primary lung cancer (cT1-2aN0M0) considered candidates for surgery and SBRT at two Japanese hospitals between October 2023 and December 2024. Patients used the PDA before finalizing treatment through shared decision-making. Outcomes were patient-perceived utility, Decisional Conflict Scale (DCS) scores measured once after the decision, and treatment preference transitions. RESULTS: Twenty-four patients completed the PDA evaluation. All participants reported improved knowledge or understanding, 18 (75.0%) reported reduced anxiety, and 23 (95.8%) reported that the PDA was useful. Final treatment selection was SBRT in 15 (57.7%), surgery in nine (34.6%), and observation in two (7.7%), with no significant difference by histological confirmation at enrollment (p = 0.59). In the exploratory post-decision DCS analysis of 22 patients, those who underwent surgery had numerically higher uncertainty scores than those who underwent SBRT (29.2 vs. 14.9). The PDA mainly clarified preferences among initially undecided patients. CONCLUSIONS: The web-based PDA was acceptable, and participants reported improved understanding and reduced anxiety. Because the DCS was administered only after treatment selection, its effect on decisional conflict could not be evaluated. Controlled evaluation of PDA-supported shared decision-making for early-stage NSCLC is warranted. TRIAL REGISTRATION: UMIN Clinical Trials Registry, UMIN000052599.

papers.abstract_en: Non-small cell lung cancer shows wide variability in outcomes after curative-intent resection. 18F-FDG PET/CT is indispensable for staging but primarily reflects glucose metabolism rather than the invasion-related tumor biology that may contribute to recurrence. 68Ga-NOTA-AE105 PET/CT images the urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor (uPAR), a cell-surface mediator of local invasion and metastatic spread. We assessed whether preoperative 68Ga-uPAR PET/CT is prognostic for postoperative recurrence. Methods: We conducted a single-center cohort study of patients with resectable lung adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma who were prospectively enrolled to undergo preoperative 68Ga-uPAR PET/CT in addition to standard-of-care 18F-FDG PET/CT. Primary tumor SUVmean and SUVmax were measured for both tracers, and tumor tissue uPAR expression was quantified by immunohistochemistry (H-score). Postoperative recurrence was the primary endpoint and was analyzed in a competing-risks framework with death as a competing event. The primary prognostic analyses evaluated 68Ga-uPAR SUVs, 18F-FDG SUVs, and uPAR H-score as continuous variables using univariable cause-specific Cox models. A 1.5-y horizon was used for exploratory Youden-derived high versus low groups, for which cumulative incidence of recurrence was estimated using the Aalen-Johansen method. Trial registration number is NCT02755675 Results: Thirty-seven patients comprised the analysis cohort, of whom 14 developed recurrence during a median follow-up of 2.38 y (interquartile range, 1.97-8.20 y). Four patients died without prior recurrence. 68Ga-uPAR uptake correlated with tumor tissue uPAR expression, whereas 18F-FDG uptake did not. As continuous prognostic factors, higher 68Ga-uPAR SUVmax (hazard ratio, 2.16; 95% CI, 1.34-3.49; P = 0.002) and higher uPAR H-score (hazard ratio, 1.04 per unit; 95% CI, 1.01-1.08; P = 0.017) were associated with recurrence; 68Ga-uPAR SUVmean showed borderline evidence of association (P = 0.053), whereas 18F-FDG uptake was not prognostic. Exploratory 1.5-y threshold analyses showed greater early recurrence in the high SUVmean and high H-score groups; the SUVmax comparison did not reach statistical significance. Conclusion: Preoperative 68Ga-uPAR PET uptake reflected tumor uPAR expression and was associated with early postoperative recurrence, whereas 18F-FDG uptake was not prognostic in this cohort. These findings suggest that uPAR PET captures invasion-related tumor biology that is not fully reflected by glucose metabolism imaging. External validation is required.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Evidence on pneumonitis after thoracic radiotherapy following immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) exposure remains limited. We examined associations with voxel-wise EQD2 mean lung dose (MLDEQD2) and the ICI-radiotherapy interval. METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort included 98 patients in a 90-day competing-risk analysis of grade ≥2 radiation pneumonitis (CTCAE), comprising 26 pneumonitis events, 70 event-free observations, and two deaths before pneumonitis. Archived DICOM doses were converted voxel-wise using α/β = 3 Gy. Cumulative incidence was estimated using the Aalen-Johansen method, and Fine-Gray regression included continuous MLDEQD2 and treatment interval. Supplementary logistic analyses included 96 patients. RESULTS: The 90-day pneumonitis cumulative incidence was 26.5% (95% CI 17.7%-35.3%). The adjusted subdistribution hazard ratio (SHR) for MLDEQD2 was 1.339 per Gy (95% CI 1.113-1.612; P = 0.002). The interval SHR was 0.784 per 10 days (95% CI 0.639-0.963; P = 0.020). Physical MLD showed a consistent association (SHR 1.197 per Gy, 95% CI 1.036-1.382; P = 0.015). CONCLUSION: Higher MLDEQD2 and shorter treatment intervals were associated with grade ≥2 symptomatic pneumonitis in this treatment sequence. Clinical ascertainment and dose-reconstruction uncertainties limit interpretation. The absence of an ICI-naive comparator precludes conclusions about ICI-specific radiosensitization. Prospective validation is required before these associations can inform dose constraints or treatment scheduling.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Gastric cancer (GC) remains a lethal malignancy with high heterogeneity and poor prognosis. Crotonylation, a key post-translational modification, contributes significantly to oncogenic processes and immune system interactions; however, its prognostic significance in gastric cancer is not fully understood. METHODS: We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing and bulk transcriptomics to evaluate cell-specific crotonylation activity and utilized WGCNA to identify core crotonylation-related gene modules. A machine learning-derived crotonylation-related prognostic signature (CRGS) was established and validated across independent cohorts. Functional enrichment, immune infiltration, and immunotherapy response analyses were conducted. Furthermore, the expression and oncogenic roles of a key risk gene, TIMP1, were experimentally validated using qRT-PCR, colony formation, and Transwell migration/invasion assays. RESULTS: Single-cell analysis revealed significantly elevated crotonylation activity in epithelial cells. The machine learning-derived CRGS successfully stratified patients into distinct risk groups, with high-risk patients showing a severe survival disadvantage. The nomogram integrating the CRGS and clinical factors demonstrated robust prognostic accuracy. Functional analysis indicated that high-risk patients were enriched in tumor-promoting pathways, while low-risk patients exhibited enhanced immune infiltration and metabolic homeostasis. The low-risk group also exhibited elevated tumor mutational burden, stronger cancer-immunity cycle activity, and better predicted response to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Experimental validation confirmed that TIMP1 was heavily upregulated in GC cell lines. Silencing TIMP1 significantly suppressed GC cell proliferation, colony formation, migration, and invasion. CONCLUSIONS: Our study establishes a reliable, clinically translatable CRGS for risk stratification and immunotherapy prediction, while identifying TIMP1 as a potential therapeutic target and a key oncogenic factor in vitro in GC.

papers.abstract_en: T cells recognize antigens from pathogens and transformed cells. Yet what antigen is "ideal"? We propose a theoretical framework in which recognition is governed by T cell selection maximized near, not far from, self. Genomic errors generate antigens closer to self that paradoxically overlap with pathogen antigens and are immunogenic and non-self. We formalize this concept as the Neoantigen Quality Model, recasting antigen recognition as an adaptation to surveil the self and non-self living worlds.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Tripartite motif-containing (TRIM) proteins are important RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligases that regulate protein fate and signal transduction through ubiquitin/ubiquitin-like modifications and non-ubiquitination mechanisms. In digestive system cancers, TRIM proteins exert highly context-dependent bidirectional effects. Here, we conceptualize TRIM proteins as signal integration nodes linking ubiquitin-mediated regulation, core signaling pathways, and adaptation to the tumor microenvironment. METHODS: This structured narrative review synthesizes English-language studies indexed in PubMed between January 2010 and October 2025. It focuses on the structural basis, multilevel regulation, molecular networks, phenotypic functions, prognostic relevance, and therapeutic implications of TRIM proteins in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, gastric cancer, colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. CONCLUSIONS: The modular architecture of TRIM proteins enables diverse substrate recognition and regulatory outputs. Cross-cancer analysis identifies pathway-convergent, phenotype-convergent, and pathway-phenotype bridging TRIM members that translate dysregulation of core pathways, including Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT, and p53, into proliferative, cell death-related, metastatic, metabolic, and immune phenotypes. Their functional direction is jointly shaped by tumor type, molecular subtype, substrate status, microenvironmental cues, and treatment context. Selected TRIM members show potential as prognostic biomarkers, risk-stratification indicators, and predictors of therapeutic response, whereas most TRIM-targeted strategies remain preclinical. Future studies should clarify ubiquitin-chain-specific regulatory logic, subtype-specific functions, and multilayered networks, while rigorously evaluating the specificity, safety, and clinical applicability of TRIM-directed combination therapies.

papers.abstract_en: Lymph node metastasis (LNM) in bladder cancer (BCa) is associated with poor clinical outcomes and may contribute to the development of metastatic tolerance, yet the stromal mechanisms underlying this process remain incompletely understood. By integrating single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, clinical cohorts, and functional models, we identified an LNM-enriched matrix-remodeling cancer-associated fibroblast (matCAF) state characterized by LRRC15 and POSTN expression and associated with adverse survival and reduced immunotherapy response. Mechanistically, Hybrid_CCND1⁺ malignant epithelial cells promoted matCAF differentiation through FOS-dependent TGFB1 transcription and TGF-β1-TGFBR1-RUNX2 signaling. Spatial analyses further revealed barrier-like accumulation of matCAFs at tumor-stroma interfaces and linked matCAF-rich neighborhoods to enhanced PI3K activity and lymphangiogenesis-related programs. Functionally, matCAF-derived POSTN engaged ITGAV/ITGB5 to activate PI3K-AKT signaling and promote tumor and lymphatic endothelial remodeling. MatCAFs were also associated with SPP1⁺ macrophage remodeling and impaired CD8⁺ T-cell function, partly through RUNX2-associated CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling. Pharmacological disruption of the RUNX2-dependent matCAF program reduced tumor burden and partially restored T-cell activity in vivo. Collectively, these findings identify matCAF-centered stromal remodeling as a potential cellular basis of the metastatic-tolerance niche in BCa LNM and provide proof-of-concept for therapeutic targeting of the matCAF program.

papers.abstract_en: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to explore the effects of circ_FAM210A on the migration and invasion of NSCLC cells through the miR-670-5p/SYNE3/apoptotic pathway axis. METHODS: The expressions of circ_FAM210A, miR-670-5p, and SYNE3 in NSCLC cells and tissues were analysed using RT‒qPCR. circ_FAM210A was characterized by Sanger sequencing, actinomycin D treatment, and RNA digestion assays. Nuclear‒cytoplasmic separation and FISH were performed to determine the distribution of circ_FAM210A. Cell models of NSCLC (A549 and H1299) were established. The effects of upregulation of circ_FAM210A expression and downregulation of miR-670-5p expression on the malignant progression of NSCLC were assessed via plate colony formation, cell scratch repair, chamber assays, apoptosis analysis, and protein band detection. The interactions between miR-670-5p and SYNE3 or circ_FAM210A were examined using dual-luciferase and RIP assays. Rescue experiments were conducted to analyse the regulatory effect of the circ_FAM210A/miR-670-5p/SYNE3 axis on NSCLC development. In vivo experiments were conducted to explore the effect of circ_FAM210A on tumours in mice. RESULTS: In NSCLC cells and tissues, the expression of circ_FAM210A and SYNE3 decreased, whereas the expression of miR-670-5p significantly increased. Circ_FAM210A is highly stable and is mostly distributed in the cytoplasm of A549 and H1299 cells. Both the downregulation of miR-670-5p expression and the overexpression of circ_FAM210A inhibited the proliferation, migration and invasion of NSCLC cells and promoted apoptosis as well as the activity of apoptotic signals. miR-670-5p directly binds to circ_FAM210A and SYNE3. The inhibition of SYNE3 reversed the cell inhibition mediated by miR-670-5p knockdown. Furthermore, overexpression of miR-670-5p or knockdown of SYNE3 abrogated the suppressive effects of circ_FAM210A on NSCLC growth and invasion. In vivo experiments demonstrated that upregulation of circ_FAM210A expression reduced both the size and weight of tumours in mice. CONCLUSION: Upregulation of circ_FAM210A expression can inhibit the malignant progression of NSCLC, partly through the miR-670-5p/SYNE3/apoptotic pathway axis.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Breast cancer develops within a metabolically heterogeneous tumor microenvironment characterized by regional hypoxia, glycolytic activation, lactate accumulation, extracellular acidification, and impaired antitumor immunity. Lactate is now recognized not only as a metabolic end product, but also as a transported substrate, a receptor ligand, and a potential source of lysine lactylation. MAIN BODY: In this Review, we summarize current evidence on lactate production, MCT1/MCT4-dependent trafficking, GPR81/HCAR1-mediated sensing, immune remodeling, and metabolic-epigenetic regulation in breast cancer. We organize these effects into three interconnected layers. First, extracellular acidification, nutrient competition, and redox stress produce rapid and potentially reversible suppression of CD8⁺ T cells, natural killer cells, and dendritic cells. Second, sustained lactate-rich conditions alter the relative fitness of immune and stromal populations, weakening cytotoxic effectors while supporting regulatory T cells, tumor-associated macrophages, suppressive myeloid populations, and stromal immune exclusion. Third, histone and non-histone lactylation, together with RNA-level and chromatin regulatory mechanisms, may contribute to more durable state fixation. We distinguish direct breast cancer evidence from mechanisms established in other cancers and from transcriptome-based lactylation-associated signatures. We also discuss methodological limitations, subtype-specific evidence, and therapeutic strategies targeting lactate production, transport, sensing, and downstream epigenetic regulation. SHORT CONCLUSION: Lactate-driven metabolic and epigenetic regulation provides a useful framework for understanding immune evasion and therapeutic resistance in breast cancer. However, direct mechanistic evidence remains concentrated in triple-negative breast cancer and tumor-intrinsic phenotypes. Lactylation should therefore be considered a candidate mechanism of durable state fixation rather than a universal explanation for lactate-associated effects. Future studies integrating direct lactylation measurements, spatial multi-omics, functional perturbation, and patient-derived models will be required to define clinically actionable lactate-dependent states.
